text: The bank robberies are paying for a dancer's career, and that is the whole of the motive. Under the science fiction sits an arrangement of exactly that size: a library clerk, an experiment that failed, and a man who can thin himself into vapor deciding the power is for someone else's recital. Ninety-two minutes, Tokyo, 1960. The difficulty is procedural — every tool the police have assumes a body that stays where it is put, and a cordon means nothing to a thing that moves like weather. Honda keeps the crimes domestic in scale: the money has a destination, and the killing falls on whoever stands between the man and it. The genre furniture is familiar. What the film does with the room left over is give its monster an address, a job he used to hold, and a person he answers to.

The war is nearly over, and the orders coming down have begun to assume that a man is a component. Okamoto's soldier has served the whole of it without a flicker of doubt, which is what makes him useful to officers who have run short of everything except men. He does what he is told. What he is told keeps getting stranger, until one order puts him inside a one-man submarine aimed at the hull of an enemy ship — a weapon whose design contains its own conclusion, treated here less as horror than as paperwork that happened to arrive. The film is filed as a comedy and it is one, in the way that a joke told at the wrong volume is one. Made in 1968, at a generation's distance from what it describes.

Two detectives take a room across from a woman they have nothing on, and begin to watch her. The suspicion is thin — a murderer might, eventually, come back to someone he once loved — and Nomura gives 116 minutes to the interval that thinness opens. What fills it is a household seen from outside: who leaves, at what hour, carrying what, and what two salaried men make of that as the days stack up. The equipment is eyes, a notebook, and the work of not being remarked on. Discomfort accumulates without ever being announced, because the woman has done nothing and is being studied anyway, on the chance that someone else still wants her. A 1958 crime picture that puts nearly all its weight on waiting is making a wager about attention: that a viewer will start noticing the same small things the watchers do.

A man past seventy is on his way back to the house he grew up in, and the film happens mostly behind his eyes. Kinoshita builds the 1955 picture out of that gap — an old traveler in the present, a boy and a girl some sixty years behind him, and the distance between them treated as the subject rather than as a device for getting to a love story. The remembered part is early: the age at which a household's rules about who may speak to whom still feel like weather rather than policy. Almost nothing happens loudly. The film is exact about how little the two are permitted and how much passes anyway, and it declines to settle whether an old man's version of a girl is the truest account anyone has or a thing he built.

The parents are not shocked that their son embezzled; they are worried that the sums are visible. In 1962 Kawashima put an entire household on one side of the ledger — the theft is a family asset now, and protecting it is a chore handled between meals, alongside whatever else the house has running. Ninety-six minutes is barely enough to establish that everyone within reach is working an angle, and the film spends them proving that this family are not even the most capable operators in their own story. The wit lives in manners: bowing, tea, careful phrasing, all of it required to keep working while the numbers move. Nobody says what they mean. Everyone understands perfectly. Money is the only thing in the room that behaves honestly; it can be counted.

The building exists to be forgotten: rooms rented by the hour, no names asked, nothing meant to outlast the night. Sōmai puts two people into one of those rooms in 1985 — Yumi, who works as a call girl, and Tetsuro, who owes money to the yakuza. What happens between them is violent and short, and by every design of the place it should have vanished at checkout. It does not. The film's subject is the years after: two people with every reason to forget each other finding that the one night neither can account for is the only fixed thing in either life. Eighty-eight minutes, most of it at the scale of a single room, with money running under every exchange — the debt, the fee, the hourly rate.

Three people in an Osaka flat live on what one of them can earn an hour at a time. The daughter works; the mother worked and is aging out of it; the brother, who cannot manage alone, is why the arithmetic never balances. Tanaka's 1974 film runs eighty-three minutes and has little plot beyond that: rent, food, the next customer, the low constant negotiation of who owes what inside a family that is also a business. The mid-seventies city appears only as far as the rooms and the streets between them require. What keeps this from being a case study is the daughter, who is written as nobody's victim; the film hands her the run of her own decisions, including the poor ones.

Tokyo, 1934: a clan's leadership falls vacant, the obvious successor is offered it, and he says no. Everything in the ninety-five minutes that follow comes out of that refusal, because an organization running on rank and obligation has no procedure for a man who will not take what he is owed. Yamashita treats succession the way another picture would treat a robbery: a plan with steps, each of which can fail. The pleasure is in watching men who are not permitted to say plainly what they want use rank and etiquette to say it anyway. Gambling is the business; the transactions that matter are obligations no ledger records. The film takes the code seriously enough to show precisely where the code stops being able to help anyone.

The case opens with a death the police have no authority over: a teenage boy, by his own hand, no crime in it. Then people who knew him start dying, and the detectives in Katō's 1968 film find themselves working backwards from someone's reasoning rather than forwards from evidence. The labels never settle — thriller, horror, crime, drama — which is roughly what watching it feels like. One half is procedural and cold. The other belongs to whoever is doing the killing, and the film is willing to make that logic legible without making it agreeable, which is the harder job. The question it keeps returning to is not the name at the end of the investigation. It is what was done to a boy before anyone thought to ask him anything.

A marine park is coming, and the land it needs belongs to a logger who speaks of the mountain as though it can hear him. Yanagimachi gives that collision 125 minutes, long enough that neither party gets to be simply right. Tatsuo cuts trees for a living and defends the forest's sacredness in the same breath, and the film treats it not as hypocrisy but as the ordinary condition of a man who lives by taking from what he reveres. His resistance is neither organized nor civic. It is personal and boorish, aimed at neighbors as often as at developers, and the film gives it room without giving it cover. The scale stays small throughout: a coastline, a work crew, a few families obliged to keep speaking to each other afterward. That an objector is allowed no clean hands is what keeps this out of pamphlet territory.

The revenge of the 47 Ronin sits at the edge of this film rather than at its center. Mori takes two men who like each other, puts one in Lord Asano's orbit and the other among Lord Kira's people, and follows what a quarrel between great houses does to a friendship neither wants to give up. The large story's outcome is common knowledge, which frees the picture from suspense and lets it spend 109 minutes on obligation instead: what a retainer owes, to whom, and how long two people can keep meeting once the answer stops being the same for both. The swordwork, when it arrives, is a consequence of rank and paperwork. What is unusual in a 1959 period film about loyalty is how much of it concerns the cost of being fond of the wrong person.

The errand is to persuade an actual film star to appear in a picture two amateurs have not made yet. Tsuboi and Kinoshita step off a train at a country station with nothing waiting for them, and Yamashita films the journey at the speed a journey like that actually moves: schedules, dead hours, and the particular awkwardness of two friends who have run out of things to say and cannot go home yet. The year is 2004, and not one event in it is large enough to summarize. The comedy is dry to the point of being deniable, made of timing and silence more than of lines, and it asks for a viewer willing to watch two people be mildly disappointed at length. What sits underneath is plain: most of any small ambition gets spent traveling to a meeting the other party has not confirmed.

A matchmaker seats a Tokyo family of some standing across from a man who repairs cars for a living, and the arrangement is meant to proceed from there. Kinoshita made this in 1949, four years into a country putting itself back together, and the comedy runs on two incompatible ideas of worth: a household that knows how to receive a guest, and a man whose money came out of engines and grease and who cannot pretend otherwise. The touch is light throughout. Everyone is courteous; almost nothing is stated; the actual negotiation has to be read off the small adjustments people make in each other's company. The film's sympathy does not sit only with the man crossing the distance — the young woman is given something to weigh, and time to weigh it.

The investigator turns up with a press card and no intention of filing anything. Okubo's brother died at a Japanese outpost in northern China — not in battle, at somebody's hand — and the only way a stranger gets onto a military post is to arrive as a war correspondent with harmless questions. Okamoto builds the film out of that device: an inquiry conducted inside an army, where every man who has an answer outranks the man asking for it, and where the war itself sits in the background as a condition rather than a cause. The frontier shape is deliberate — an isolated garrison, a stranger riding in, a unit that has made its own rules while nobody was looking. Made in 1959, when choosing a murder at an outpost as the subject, rather than the war around it, was itself a position.
